title: More Brightener, Less White: Five Optical Brightening Mistakes that Cost Process Houses Whiteness
description: Read article about The article explains five OBA mistakes that reduce whiteness, waste chemicals, raise effluent load, and shows how process houses can control whites under D65. and more articles about Textile industary at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Optical brighteners improve whiteness by adding blue fluorescence, but overdosing can reduce fluorescence, create a greenish tint, waste chemicals, and increase effluent load.
For cotton, process houses should identify the lowest effective dose, avoid cationic carry-over and iron, and verify whether cooler, shorter cycles can meet the target.
Check whites under D65.
markdown:
A buyer decides whether a white shirt is acceptable in about a second. If it has even a faint cream cast, it looks old. That is why optical brightening agents (OBAs), also called fluorescent whitening agents, sit in almost every recipe for white cotton, linen, polyester and blends. OBAs absorb invisible ultraviolet light at roughly 330–380 nm and re-emit it as visible blue light at about 400–450 nm. Bleaching removes colour. An OBA adds blue light, which cancels the residual yellowness of bleached fabric and makes it look brighter.

Because the effect is optical rather than chemical, it behaves differently from bleaching, and the habits that work in a bleach bath often backfire in a brightening bath. Published research points to five common mistakes.

Treating OBA like Bleach: More is not Whiter

With peroxide, a stronger bath usually gives a whiter fabric, at least until fibre damage sets in. An OBA does not work that way. Whiteness climbs steeply at low doses, levels off and then falls.

Hussain and co-workers (2012) measured this on cotton with a stilbene brightener. Untreated fabric had a CIE whiteness index of 80.6. At 0.15 per cent on the weight of fabric (owf), the index rose to 145.5. At 0.25 per cent it was 144.1, and at 0.50 per cent it fell to 140.0. Above the optimum, the extra brightener molecules cluster together on the fibre, fluoresce less and start to absorb violet light themselves. The fabric then turns slightly green. In other words, the extra chemical made the fabric less white.

Other studies agree. Miljković et al. (2020) got the highest whiteness on cotton with Uvitex BHT at just 0.1 per cent, almost twice the whiteness that hydrogen peroxide bleaching alone achieved. Dekanić et al. (2020) found that the fluorescence of common brighteners in solution dropped sharply at concentrations of 2 per cent and above.

Practical Point: run a short dose ladder for each OBA and fabric quality, for example 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 per cent owf. Lock in the lowest dose that reaches your whiteness target. The optimum for most cotton brighteners lies somewhere between 0.1 and 0.5 per cent owf.

Running Hotter and Longer than Needed

Supplier data sheets are written to work across many machines and water qualities, so they tend to be generous. For Uvitex BHT, the manufacturer's range quoted by Dekanić et al. (2020) is 80–90 °C for 60 minutes at pH 7–12. The same researchers ran a deliberately shorter and cooler cycle of 60 °C for 30 minutes at neutral pH. They still obtained satisfactory whiteness and effective UV protection on cotton.

For a process house, every 20–30 °C and every half hour cut from a bath saves steam, water heating and machine time. It is worth confirming on your own fabric whether the supplier’s full cycle is really needed.

Ignoring what else is in the Bath

Most anionic stilbene brighteners for cotton behave like direct dyes. Other chemicals in the bath can quietly undo their effect.

•   Cationic Products. Tutak (2011) found that cationised cotton brightened to a lower whiteness index than untreated cotton, with a blue-green rather than a reddish tint. Cationic softeners and fixing agents carried over into the OBA bath can cause the same kind of loss.

•   Iron and Other Metal Ions. Iron ions quench the fluorescence of stilbene and biphenyl brighteners in solution (Dekanić et al., 2021). Water quality and a suitable sequestering agent therefore matter.

•   Residual Peroxide and Alkali. An OBA can only add to the whiteness already achieved in pretreatment, so the fabric needs to be well rinsed and neutralised after bleaching.

Practical Point: keep cationic finishes out of the brightening bath or apply them afterwards, and check the iron content of your process water before blaming the brightener.

On Polyester, Temperature does Most of the Work

Polyester has no ionic sites. Disperse-type brighteners such as OB-1 only enter the fibre when it is heated well above its glass transition temperature, much as disperse dyes do. Cai et al. (2023) optimised the whitening of polyester with a fine OB-1 dispersion and found that temperature accounted for 93.87 per cent of the variation in whiteness. Time contributed 2.07 per cent and brightener amount just 1.65 per cent. Their best result came at 130 °C.

The lesson for the shop floor is that adding more OBA cannot make up for a bath that does not reach temperature. If polyester whites come out dull, check the temperature profile before increasing the dose.

Judging White Under the Wrong Light

An OBA only works when ultraviolet light is present. Daylight and the standard D65 illuminant contain UV-A, but many warm LED and tungsten lamps contain very little. A shirt that looks brilliant at the window can look ordinary under shop lighting, and two lots can match in one booth and differ in another. The whiteness you see depends directly on the UV content of the light falling on it, which is why whiteness measurement relies on careful control of the UV content of the instrument’s light source (Datacolor, n.d.).

For dependable approval:

•   Compare samples in a light cabinet under D65, then check them under a UV lamp, which shows uneven brightener as streaks or patches.

•   Measure instrumentally with a spectrophotometer that includes the UV component and is calibrated with a fluorescent standard, following ISO 105-J02 or AATCC TM110. Recalibrate the UV setting regularly; Datacolor recommends weekly.

•   Report both the CIE whiteness index and the whiteness tint (Tw). A Tw between −3 and +3 is considered neutral. Positive values indicate a greenish tint and negative values a reddish one (Tutak, 2011). A rising Tw is an early warning of over-dosing.

Why it Matters Beyond the Fabric

OBAs are designed to be stable, which makes them hard to remove from wastewater. Poiger et al. (1996) measured the two most common detergent brighteners at 7–21 µg/L in primary sewage effluent, 2.6–8.9 µg/L after secondary treatment and 0.04–0.57 µg/L in river water. Brighteners are highly water-soluble and poorly biodegradable, and much of them passes through biological treatment (Assaad et al., 2014).

Every gram of brightener that does not end up on the fabric is money paid for chemicals that go down the drain and add to the effluent load. The steps that give the best whiteness, namely the right dose, high exhaustion, a clean bath and correct temperature, also give the lowest cost and the smallest environmental footprint.

Quick Checklist

1.  Run a dose ladder and use the lowest dose that meets the target, typically 0.1–0.5 per cent owf on cotton.

2. Trial a shorter and cooler cycle against the data-sheet recipe.

3. Keep cationic chemicals out of the OBA bath and control iron in the water.

4. On polyester, fix the temperature profile before raising the dose.

5. Approve whites under D65 with a UV-calibrated spectrophotometer, tracking both whiteness index and tint.
